title: 1 Samuel 18:1–5
context: After the victory, Jonathan, Saul’s son and heir, loves David as his own soul and makes a covenant with him, giving David his robe, armor, sword, bow and sash. Saul keeps David at court and sets him over the men of war, and David acts wisely wherever he is sent. Many interpreters see Jonathan’s gifts as a sign that the heir apparent recognizes David’s future, a theme made explicit later (23:17). These verses also belong to the material absent from the shorter Septuagint form. Both traditions see covenant friendship and self-giving loyalty here, and see God’s purpose for David advancing through human love and faithfulness.

verses.text: When he had finished speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
verses.arminianNotes:
When David finishes speaking with Saul, Jonathan’s soul is knit with David’s, and Jonathan loves him as his own soul. A deep friendship begins.

Arminian readers note that Jonathan’s love is freely given; he chooses loyalty to David even though David’s rise threatens his own claim to the throne, an example of love that seeks another’s good.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God provides David with a loyal friend at the very time Saul’s hostility is about to grow, a mark of providential care for his chosen servant. These verses are among those absent from the shorter Septuagint form.

Both traditions honor Jonathan’s covenant love as a model of faithful friendship.

verses.text: Saul took him that day, and wouldn’t let him go home to his father’s house any more.
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul takes David that day and does not let him return to his father’s house. David now lives at court.

Arminian readers note that this change places David in a position of influence and danger, where his integrity will be tested by success, envy and opportunity, and where his choices will matter greatly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God moves David from the sheepfold to the palace, positioning him for the role he has been anointed to fill, even though the path will run through suffering.

Both traditions see David’s entrance into Saul’s household as a step in God’s purpose, and as a place of both honor and peril.

verses.text: Then Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan and David make a covenant, because Jonathan loves him as his own soul. The friendship is formalized.

Arminian readers note that covenant here is a mutual commitment freely entered, and that faithfulness to such promises is a mark of godly character, as Jonathan’s later loyalty will show (20:8, 42).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the covenant between Jonathan and David reflects, on a human level, the covenant loyalty that marks God’s dealings with his people, and that it will later bear fruit in David’s kindness to Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9:1, 7).

Both traditions see this covenant as an act of steadfast love.

verses.text: Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was on him and gave it to David with his clothing, even including his sword, his bow, and his sash.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan takes off his robe and gives it to David with his clothing, sword, bow and sash. The heir gives his royal gear to David.

Arminian readers note that Jonathan’s gift is a voluntary act of humility, as he honors the one God has favored, and many interpreters see it as a symbolic yielding of his own claim (compare 23:17).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the gifts may signify Jonathan’s recognition of God’s choice of David, and that Jonathan submits his natural expectations to God’s purpose, an example of faith that embraces God’s will even at personal cost.

Both traditions read Jonathan’s gesture as remarkable self-giving, while recognizing that its full symbolic meaning is interpreted variously.

verses.text: David went out wherever Saul sent him, and behaved himself wisely; and Saul set him over the men of war. It was good in the sight of all the people, and also in the sight of Saul’s servants.
verses.arminianNotes:
David goes wherever Saul sends him and acts wisely, so Saul puts him over the men of war, and it pleases all the people and Saul’s servants. David succeeds in everything.

Arminian readers note that David’s wisdom in serving Saul is a matter of his own faithful conduct, and that success that comes from godly behavior wins the trust of others.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s success is credited in this chapter to the LORD being with him (18:12, 14, 28), so his wise conduct is the outworking of God’s favor. The Hebrew verb for acting wisely can also mean succeeding.

Both traditions affirm both David’s wise conduct and God’s favor as the source of his success.
